claims.text: A PVD-deposited alumina coating on boride-based components will significantly improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Conventional Fe-B or other boride-based components with established boride layers are susceptible to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The protective alumina coating should have a thickness of approximately 1–5 µm.
PVD can produce high-quality, completely dense, and well-adhered films.
Depositing the alumina coating at approximately 500–600 °C in high vacuum will ensure high purity and adhesion.
Hot-dip aluminum-plating components operate in molten aluminum at approximately 750–900 °C.
PVD deposition will create a uniform, dense, and well-adhered alumina layer covering the boride surface.
Alumina provides significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
The PVD-deposited alumina film is chemically inert and thermally stable in contact with molten aluminum at 750–900 °C.
The alumina film prevents direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Preventing direct contact limits interdiffusion and chemical reactions at the molten-aluminum/boride interface.
Limiting interdiffusion and interfacial reactions reduces corrosive attack and material degradation.
Relative to an uncoated boride surface, the alumina-coated component will have lower weight loss, spallation, and interfacial attack during molten-aluminum exposure.
The appropriate baseline is the same boride-based component with its native boride layer but without an additional alumina coating.
Prolonged thermal cycling may impair coating adhesion.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between alumina and the boride substrate may cause delamination and limit effectiveness.
Short-term corrosion-resistance improvements are expected, whereas durability under repeated thermal cycling is uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in weight loss, spallation, or interfacial degradation relative to an uncoated control would falsify the hypothesis.
